The melting point of wustite (FeO) was measured to be around 1398°C in 5N argon atmosphere, but showed poor reproducibility and gradual shift to higher temperatures due to oxidation to magnetite (Fe3O4).
In the Ar/CO2/CO gas mixture, the measured melting points of the wustite were around 1385-1386°C, indicating that the Fe2+ valence state could be stabilized in this atmosphere up to at least 1480°C.
Olivine crystals (Mg,Fe)2SiO4 grown in 5N nitrogen contained Fe3+ inclusions of magnetite (Fe3O4), due to the too high oxygen partial pressure in the nitrogen atmosphere.
Olivine crystals grown in the Ar/CO2/CO gas mixture showed no Fe3+ inclusions, as the oxygen partial pressure was maintained within the stability region of Fe2+.
The largest single crystalline region of the wustite crystals grown by micro-pulling-down had a diameter of about 3 mm.
At very high pulling rates of 20-50 mm/min, the wustite crystal diameter self-adjusted to around 5 mm, likely due to insufficient material transport through the capillary.
X-ray powder diffraction analysis confirmed that the wustite crystals grown in the Ar/CO2/CO atmosphere were pure wustite (FeO).
The calculated oxygen partial pressure (pO2) in the Ar/CO2/CO gas mixture at 1400°C was 9.65 × 10^-9 bar, which is within the stability region of Fe2+.
The Fe/Mg ratio in the outer rim of the olivine crystals grown in the Ar/CO2/CO mixture was about 4 times higher than in the center, suggesting lower oxygen partial pressure in the Fe-enriched rim.
A Czochralski-grown forsterite (Mg2SiO4) single crystal was used as a seed to initiate the growth of the olivine (Mg,Fe)2SiO4 mixed crystals by the micro-pulling-down method.

Thermodynamic equilibrium calculations showed that the Ar/CO2/CO gas mixture could adjust the oxygen partial pressure (pO2) in a way that matched the temperature dependence needed to stabilize the Fe2+ valence state.
Pure inert gases like argon or nitrogen could not maintain the desired Fe2+ state, leading to undesired oxidation to Fe3+.
The authors used a NETZSCH STA 409C thermal analyzer with a standard SiC heater furnace and heating/cooling rates of ±10 K/min for the DTA/TG measurements.
The micro-pulling-down (μ-PD) method was used for the crystal growth experiments, with fibers pulled from iridium crucibles at rates of around 0.5 mm/min.
Iron(II) oxalate dihydrate (Fe(COO)2·2H2O) with 5N purity was used as the starting material for the growth of wustite crystals.
